description: A timeline comparison of battery pack price collapse vs. automaker momentum—tracking how fast lithium-ion got cheaper, how that changed vehicle economics, and which leaders benefited as the market scaled.
youtube_description:
🚨 Chaptered chart-race: the EV battery price collapse that reshaped every business model.

0:00 The $1,000/kWh era—why EVs weren’t “inevitable” yet
1:35 2016–2018: learning curves + scale start cutting costs fast
3:10 2019–2020: the world crosses the “it’s finally different” threshold (~$156/kWh pack)
5:05 2021–2022: supply shocks + inflation spike costs (and pressure margins)
7:15 2023–2025: continued efficiency + chemistry/manufacturing gains bring prices back down
9:00 Why Tesla accelerates with cheaper packs (revenue climb)
10:45 Why BYD capitalizes as China scales (revenue surge)
12:25 The grid side goes nuclear: storage deployment in GWh explodes
14:30 Finale: the cost curve vs. the companies that turned it into wins

If you like dramatic chart-races, hit LIKE and SUBSCRIBE—next episode: where the “battery boom” meets charging buildout.

Hashtags for discovery: #electricvehicles #ev #batterytech #energystorage #chartrace #tesla #byd #climatetech #cleanenergy #lithiumion
instagram_caption:
🚀 The $1,000/kWh shock… then the price Tsunami that rewired the EV world.

Picture 2010: a lithium‑ion battery pack costing about **$1,100/kWh**. EVs existed, but the math didn’t. Automakers were fighting for prototypes, not profits. Then the timeline starts to tilt—because costs weren’t just drifting. They were collapsing.

By **2014**, pack costs were down to roughly **$740/kWh**. In **2018**, they were around **$390/kWh**—and suddenly EV economics stopped being a “maybe” and started being a spreadsheet. The real punchline hits around **2020**: the global average lands near **$156/kWh**. That year is the inflection point for scale. Cheaper packs don’t just reduce cost—they unlock incentives, widen margins, and make manufacturers confident enough to ramp production.

But this is never a straight line. In **2022**, the world gets rocked—supply constraints and pricing pressure push packs back up to about **$151/kWh**. It’s the “wait, what happened?” chapter. Then the curve keeps improving again: around **2024 (~$112/kWh)** and into **2025 (~$98/kWh)**. That’s not just cheaper batteries—that’s a new operating system for the entire industry.

Now watch who benefits. Tesla’s selected revenue jumps from single-digit early on to **~$53B (2021)** and **~$96B (2023)**, then accelerates further to **~$122B (2025)** as costs stabilize and demand scales. BYD does something even more dramatic—rising into the **$80B+ range by 2021** and pushing to **~$155B by 2025**.

And the plot twists: the grid starts drinking the same battery revolution. Global energy storage deployment grows from tiny early levels to **~310 GWh by 2025**, meaning batteries aren’t only powering cars—they’re reshaping power systems.

🔥 Which matters more for the next EV wave: **battery costs falling faster**, or **manufacturing capacity scaling faster**? Comment your pick—and tag someone who loves chart-races.

Follow for more viral timeline comparisons—SUBSCRIBE so you don’t miss the next one.
facebook_caption:
Battery prices are not just an engineering story—they are a market-shaping event. This chart-race compares the global lithium-ion battery pack cost trajectory against the scaling outcomes of major automakers and the growth of energy storage.

The global average pack cost falls from roughly **$1,100/kWh (2010)** to about **$390/kWh (2018)**, reaching near **$156/kWh (2020)**—a widely referenced threshold that changes EV economics by enabling lower vehicle costs and faster production ramp-up. The curve then experiences turbulence: pack costs rise back toward **~$151/kWh (2022)** amid input and supply pressure, before continuing down again to approximately **$112/kWh (2024)** and **~$98/kWh (2025)** as manufacturing scale and process improvements reassert the downward trend.

Those cost shifts map to company performance in the same period. Tesla’s selected revenue profile rises strongly into **~$53B (2021)** and **~$96B (2023)**, reaching **~$122B (2025)**. BYD’s growth is even steeper in the chart: moving from a mid-decade ramp to **~$84B (2021)**, then **~$110B (2023)** and **~$155B (2025)**. Meanwhile, energy storage deployment accelerates from minimal levels to **~310 GWh by 2025**, showing the battery boom is expanding beyond vehicles into grid reliability and renewables integration.

What’s your takeaway: are we heading toward the biggest winners being those with the lowest battery costs, or those with the fastest scale?

From ~**$1,100/kWh (2010)** to ~**$156/kWh (2020)**, then a bump back around **~$151/kWh (2022)**, and down again to ~**$98/kWh (2025)**. That curve basically decides who can scale EVs profitably.

Tesla’s selected revenue climbs into **~$53B (2021)** and **~$96B (2023)**, while BYD ramps harder to **~$155B (2025)**. And the grid side goes crazy too—global storage deployment hits **~310 GWh by 2025**.

Real question: who wins next—companies with the cheapest packs, or companies with the fastest factories?
